title: UX Audit & Improvements
subtitle: Finding the friction in the shopping experience — and making meaningful improvements.

cover.alt: The Irish Store checkout on desktop and mobile search results on a phone

info.label: My role
info.value: UX Designer, working alongside two other UX designers

info.label: My involvement
info.value: User research, analysis, prototype builds and handover to developers

paragraphs: The Irish Store is an e-commerce retailer with a vision to become the destination digital retailer for products with deep emotional meaning and strong cultural connection.
The business saw a massive increase in new users during 2020 (Covid). With that rapid growth, more issues started coming to light through queries from customer service.
The business needed to address these issues to keep hold of its customers and create a better user experience.
blocks.heading: When growth brings the cracks to the surface

paragraphs: The aim was to improve the experience through “quick wins” that would also benefit the business. We started with three targets:
blocks.heading: What we set out to do

items.label: Target: decrease customer service queries and complaints

paragraphs: These were the goals we set at the start of the project, not results. The reported outcomes are in section 06.
I worked alongside two other UX designers, and was involved in the user research, analysis, prototype builds and handover to developers.
blocks.heading: How we worked

paragraphs: Before the user tests, we defined the Irish Store customer using previous data: a woman based in the USA, aged 40–60, with an income of $30,000–$100,000.

paragraphs: Most customers were happy and satisfied, and many simply said nothing needed to change. So the takeaway was to make small, considered changes that would enhance and elevate the experience.
Where people did suggest improvements, their answers fell into a few clear themes:
blocks.heading: What the survey told us

items.title: Product findability
items.why: Customers wanted clearer, more consistent product information.
points: Improve size chart information across product types, with the right context for UK and USA
Make it easier to compare items, and improve product imagery
Keep product information consistent, as some products had much more info than others
Be clear on out-of-stock items and alternatives

items.title: Basket and checkout
items.why: The payment step was causing a lot of confusion.
points: Explain the next steps and when card details will be entered
Add form hints and error messages
Make the debit card option easier to find
Be clear on discount eligibility, as codes not working caused confusion

items.title: General UX
items.why: Usability, performance and consistency came up too.
points: Usability across devices, including scrolling and freezing
Improved performance and faster page speed
Refresh the design, with consistent design patterns

paragraphs: We ran user tests across mobile, desktop and tablet, capturing what participants said, thought, did and felt.

blocks.heading: Customer needs
blocks.text: We identified two high-level customer cohorts: people buying a gift and people buying for themselves. When shopping for clothes, customers told us they consider quality and material, fit, style, price and occasion.

paragraphs: We combined insights from multiple users, from the user tests and the UX survey, into one empathy map of what customers say, think, do and feel.
Customers loved the products and described the brand as credible, authentic and trustworthy. They also found search clunky and the size guide confusing.

paragraphs: Alongside the research, we reviewed the site against UX best practice and grouped what we found into themes. Here are the main ones, and why each mattered.
blocks.heading: Reviewing the site against best practice

items.title: Navigation and terminology
items.why: If the words don’t match, customers may think they’ve clicked the wrong link.
points: Page names and navigation labels didn’t always match, for example “Sweaters” in the navigation but “Aran Jumpers” as the page title
Revisit top-level navigation and category names on the UK store (sweaters / jumpers, jewellery / jewelry)
Reduce clicks and condense categories, as some only had two products
Introduce occasion categories, such as anniversaries and milestone birthdays

items.title: Product findability
items.why: Customers need to be able to refine results easily.
points: A “find similar” pop-up got in the way on desktop and appeared mid-click, causing layout shift
Try a pricing slider, and increase tap targets on mobile facet options
Don’t show review stars on product listings for one star or below
The “find similar” button sat where people expect to find add to basket or view more

items.title: Product information and sizing
items.why: Can a user find everything they’re looking for?
points: Add a size guide for all products
Make the active promotion message and code more appealing, so it can’t be missed
Show delivery lead times on every product, not just some
Refresh the layout: justified text was hard to read, add to bag and save for later were too close together, and the quantity box needed optimising for touch

items.title: Mobile usability
items.why: On mobile, much of the information was off canvas.
points: Hard to use on iPhone 11 because a lot of the content sat off canvas
Tap targets needed attention

items.title: Basket and checkout
items.why: The checkout needed to be easy to digest, and to build trust and credibility.
points: Revisit the styling and wording, and add an image for credit and debit cards so they’re not missed
Add a message so people know card payment comes in the next step
Add a discount line to the order totals
The delivery message error appeared in the payment step with no clear action, and didn’t stay on screen
Postcode formats were inconsistent

items.title: Design consistency
items.why: A brand refresh could build trust through a consistent set of UI components.
points: Use the correct alert and message styling
Revisit calls to action, including hover states on buttons
A mix of fonts (Roboto and Roboto Condensed)
Titles switched between uppercase, mixed case and lowercase

paragraphs: After the data was presented to the stakeholders, a prioritisation session took place to go through all the recommendations in the findings.
We reviewed them through the lens of “effort required”, so that quick wins could be identified.
blocks.heading: Deciding what to tackle first

images.alt: Prioritisation matrix plotting recommendations by priority and effort, colour-coded by CX pillar
images.cap: The prioritisation matrix: recommendations plotted by priority and effort, colour-coded by CX pillar.

paragraphs: Each recommendation was placed on a matrix of priority against effort, and colour-coded by CX pillar: Customer, Acquisition, Conversion, Retention, Content, Technical and Operations.
blocks.heading: Priority versus effort

images.alt: The “My Quick Wins” board with the quick wins chosen in the prioritisation session
images.cap: The “My Quick Wins” board from the prioritisation session.

blocks.heading: The quick wins that came out of it
items: Remove the search icon from the mobile header, or increase spacing
Payment step: add credit card images and a message explaining when debit card details will be taken
Put the debit card option above PayPal
Site search: restyle the search box and A/B test it
Product pages: revisit the size guide layout and information
Show UK and USA size equivalents on each store

paragraphs: Three of the quick wins show how the research turned into design changes: the checkout, size guides and search.
blocks.heading: Three quick wins, in more detail

paragraphs: The credit card option had been stacked above PayPal. Research had shown the value of showing visuals of the cards, so we added the accepted credit cards.
We tested internally and refined the layout. From that testing, the call-to-action button was left-aligned, and the matching card icon now highlights as someone enters their card details.
Once the changes were added to the prototypes and tested further, they were handed over to the developers and implemented on the website.

paragraphs: Analysing the feedback, users wanted more information on product sizes. After reviewing the findings with stakeholders in the company, we decided the size guides would be one of the first things to update.

paragraphs: To improve the search bar, we ran an A/B test of different layouts over the course of a month. The focus was on improving the experience by designing the visuals and layout of the content.

paragraphs: These are the outcomes reported for the project, following the updated payment page. For reference, the original target for each measure was 10%.
blocks.heading: Reported results

items.label: decrease in customer queries and complaints

paragraphs: The clarification of the size guides resulted in fewer customer queries and fewer returns of wrongly sized products. These clarifications did involve some manual staff intervention, but the overall customer experience improved significantly.
blocks.heading: Size guides

paragraphs: Research, collaboration and prioritisation helped us turn usability problems into actionable improvements. Listening to customers showed us where the friction was, working with stakeholders helped us agree what to tackle first, and focusing on quick wins meant meaningful changes reached the website.
blocks.heading: What I took from it
